candidate.title: Funeral Home Impersonation Payment Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers scour online obituaries and then call or text grieving families within hours of a death, posing as the actual funeral home or director, demanding an urgent "deposit" to secure cremation or burial services.
safetyTips: Hang up and call the funeral home back using a number you already have on file or from its General Price List "not a number given in the suspicious call or text
Never send payment via wire transfer, gift card, PayPal, or Cash App for funeral services; legitimate funeral homes invoice through standard, verifiable billing
Resist pressure to pay immediately "honest businesses give you time to decide, and real funeral costs are not due within hours of a death
Limit the personal and financial details included in online obituaries, and warn family members in advance that such scam calls or texts may occur
Report suspected funeral scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to local law enforcement
candidate.howItWorks: After a death notice or obituary is posted online, fraudsters quickly search it for the deceased's name and surviving family members' contact details. They then call or text the family — often spoofing the real funeral home's phone number so the caller ID shows its actual name — claiming to be a funeral director or employee. The scammer says a payment or "deposit" is needed immediately or the cremation/burial will be canceled or delayed, pressuring the shocked, grieving family to pay right away via hard-to-trace methods like wire transfer, PayPal, or Cash App rather than the funeral home's normal billing process.
redFlags: Contact comes within hours of posting an obituary and demands immediate payment or the service will be canceled
Caller ID or texts show the real funeral home's name or number (spoofed), but payment is requested via wire transfer, PayPal, or Cash App instead of normal invoicing
Scammer pressures the family not to verify or hang up, exploiting grief and confusion
Amounts or names given by the caller don't match prior paperwork or invoices from the actual funeral home
Request to pay a third party (e.g., a 'life insurance agent' or unfamiliar name) rather than the funeral home directly
realExamples: The FTC described the scheme in a 2023 consumer alert, saying imposters pretend to be from the funeral home and claim the funeral will be canceled unless the family pays more money immediately, calling it worthy of a "Scammers Hall of Shame" top-10 spot.

NBC News reported a widow, Lisa Ann Motto, was targeted the day after her husband died, with a caller using the spoofed number of the real Rainsville Funeral Home and the name of an actual funeral director.

A Georgetown County, S.C. sheriff's office reported a mother was called by a man impersonating her son's funeral home employee demanding immediate phone payment for an "outstanding balance" right after her son's death.
In 2026, a Harlem, Georgia woman received a text from someone posing as the real funeral home owner within hours of a preliminary obituary post, after her mother's death.

triage.reasoning: This closely mirrors the existing "AI Obituary Mining 'Graveyard Grift' Scam" entry — both involve scammers scouring online obituaries to identify grieving families and then impersonating funeral homes to demand urgent deposits via spoofed calls/texts and untraceable payment methods. Without clear differentiation (e.g., no AI element emphasized here, but the core mechanism of obituary mining + funeral home impersonation + urgent deposit demand is identical), this appears to be a duplicate/variant rather than a genuinely new pattern.
